I have been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life, same as my mother before me. I know this soil, I know what sells at the grain station, and I know what my body can still manage at 57. My husband goes to the city for construction work most of the year, so I run the farm mostly alone with help from my son during harvest.

I have 8 mu of flat field. I will do what I always do — wheat in winter, maize in summer, same rotation, same field. Everyone around me does this. It works. The grain station buys both reliably. Trying new crops at my age, with no one to help me figure it out, is not worth the risk.

For wheat, I will use the Jimai 22 improved seed I get from the township agricultural supply store. It has good yield and stands up to lodging. I will apply base fertilizer before plowing — diammonium phosphate mixed with urea — then top-dress urea at jointing in April. I will irrigate three times: the winter water in November to help the seedlings survive cold, jointing water in April, and grain-filling water in May. I will spray herbicide in early spring and then do a combined fungicide-insecticide spray around heading to handle rust and aphids. I use rotary tillage every year after maize harvest, it is easier on my back than deep plowing.

For summer maize, I plant right after wheat harvest in mid-June — no time to waste, I do no-tillage and seed directly into the stubble. I use Zhengdan 958 hybrid seed, which my neighbors all use and it gives reliable yield. I apply a compound fertilizer at planting and top-dress urea when the plant is knee-high. Summer rain usually handles most of the water but I irrigate once if August is dry. I spray herbicide right after emergence and one more time mid-season for corn borer if I see it.

I expect around 450 kg/mu from wheat and 550 from maize. Not the highest in the village, but steady. That is what matters to me now.

I use improved wheat seed (Jimai 22) and hybrid maize seed (Zhengdan 958), both widely adopted locally and available from the township supply store. Fertilizer rates are set at the conventional local standard — somewhat above agronomic optimum but that is what I am used to and I cannot afford a bad year.
